content: Oat sensitivity refers to an adverse reaction to the proteins found in oats, specifically Avena sativa. This sensitivity can manifest as an allergic response to oat proteins, either through inhalation or ingestion. In some individuals with gluten-sensitive enteropathy, there is also a reaction to avenin, a protein in oats that is structurally similar to gluten found in wheat. Oat Allergy Research has shown that oat proteins can act as allergens affecting both the respiratory system and the skin. For example, studies on farmers exposed to grain dust and children with atopic dermatitis have demonstrated that oat proteins can trigger allergic reactions. Among farmers with grain dust allergies, 53% showed sensitivity to oat dust, a rate second only to barley (70%) and nearly double that of wheat dust. A specific 66 kDa protein in oats was identified in 84% of tested sera, though some of this binding may be non-specific, resembling lectin-like interactions. However, IgA and IgG responses, such as those seen in celiac disease or dermatitis herpetiformis, are not observed in atopic dermatitis patients exposed to avenins. Food allergies to oats can also co-occur with atopic dermatitis. Avenins in oats share similarities with γand ω-gliadins of wheat, which may contribute to both enteropathic and anaphylactic responses in susceptible individuals. Avenin-Sensitive Enteropathy Gluten-sensitive enteropathy (GSE), including its severe form, celiac disease, leads to inflammation of the small intestine, eventually causing villus atrophy. The disease progresses from increased lymphocyte counts to villus flattening and crypt hyperplasia. Historically, oats were thought to cause celiac disease, but this was largely due to contamination with wheat, barley, or rye. A small percentage (6%) of the celiac population may react to oats. Immunological Evidence In 1992, six oat proteins, including prolamins such as gamma avenin, were identified as reactive with celiac sera. Follow-up studies revealed that most celiac patients produce anti-avenin antibodies (AVA) with specificity and sensitivity comparable to anti-gliadin antibodies. However, AVA levels decrease when wheat gluten is removed from the diet, suggesting that oats alone may not sustain celiac disease unless wheat is also present. A study of 136 individuals on an oat diet showed a decline in AVA levels, but an increased number of intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) was observed in the oat-eating cohort. Cellular Immunity In GSE, prolamins interact with T-cells and antigen-presenting cells, while anti-transglutaminase antibodies contribute to autoimmunity. In a study of 16 celiac patients, no significant Th1 response to avenins was detected, suggesting that avenins may not play a major role in celiac disease or that the sample size was too small to detect rare responders. However, a 2004 study identified four patients with symptoms after oat ingestion, three of whom had elevated Marsh scores and avenin-responsive T-cells, indicating avenin-sensitive enteropathy (ASE). These patients had specific genetic markers (HLA DR3-DQ2/DR7-DQ2) associated with severe forms of GSE and a higher risk of complications. Synthetic avenin peptides, both native and deamidated, were tested, with deamidated forms showing stronger immune responses. The dominant immune region was identified through trypsin digestion of avenin, and activation required transglutaminase. Preliminary studies suggest that different oat strains may carry varying risks for avenin sensitivity. Oats and Celiac Disease Recent studies indicate that most children and adults with celiac disease tolerate oats well. Long-term studies (1, 2, and 5 years) on individuals consuming uncontaminated oats as part of a gluten-free diet showed no significant changes in intestinal morphology or relapse of celiac disease. Anti-gliadin and reticulin antibodies, as well as IEL counts, did not differ significantly between oat-eating celiacs and non-oat-eating controls in remission. In vitro tests sensitive to wheat gluten found that avenin peptides did not induce EMA production in cultured duodenal mucosa from celiac patients. Algorithms predicting T-cell stimulatory peptides in gluten identified many in hordeins and secalins but not in oat avenins. There is no evidence that oats alone can trigger GSE. However, in a small subset of celiac patients, oats may sustain or reactivate the disease if it was initially triggered by wheat. A recent study found higher IEL counts in oat-eating celiacs in remission, but anti-avenin antibody levels remained low as long as the diet was gluten-free. Some celiacs, approximately 5-20% of the GSE population, may respond adversely to oats. Non-compliance with a gluten-free diet, including oats, increases the risk of refractory disease and associated cancers.
